A rotator cuff tear is most likely given the hallmark painful arc, night pain, and disproportionate external rotation deficit (infraspinatus/supraspinatus involvement); MRI confirmation would be definitive. Adhesive capsulitis is highly plausible due to global restriction (though external rotation is typically *most* affected early), insidious onset, and severe night pain—but usually shows more uniform loss across all planes, and passive ROM is often equally limited without sharp pain at end-range (here, pain is prominent, suggesting active tissue pathology rather than pure capsular contracture). Calcific tendinopathy fits the inflammatory nocturnal pain and functional impairment; it commonly affects supraspinatus and causes severe, disproportionate external rotation pain due to impingement of calcified deposits. Subacromial impingement is a common precursor or coexisting condition, especially with repetitive overhead activity, but typically presents with less profound passive ROM loss unless chronic/advanced. Glenohumeral OA is less likely in absence of crepitus, age-related degenerative features, or radiographic evidence; isolated external rotation loss is atypical, and OA usually spares early passive ROM. The entropy reflects moderate uncertainty due to overlapping features among top four diagnoses, though the high-confidence separation of the top two supports focused imaging (MRI or diagnostic US) and possibly intra-articular injection response."}
